name: Dana Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play clarinet with a chamber orchestra, prepare parts for two ensembles and teach older beginners on Wednesdays. My music degree helps with the scores, but most of my day is listening for the moment a player cannot breathe through a phrase.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What makes that day work at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner handles the early school pickup when I rehearse. We have two children and a mortgage, so I keep a calendar of actual paid calls rather than assuming every invitation becomes a fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our players that a faster mailing list is useful, but it cannot rehearse a difficult entrance. I would keep asking the manager which dates carry a fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our higher musician pay and nine months of expenses saved make the mortgage manageable. Even so, an ensemble can cancel a concert after I have arranged childcare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This season I would keep the chamber rehearsals, part preparation and Wednesday lessons. I use AI occasionally to draft a concert note, then check names and programme dates against the signed sheet before it goes out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about last-minute cancellations, even without an AI shock. The plateau would leave my usual work intact.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened with the last cancelled concert?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We lost the winter concert to a hall closure. The manager paid the rehearsal fee, and I will ask for that cancellation term in writing before the next contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children that evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell them the empty hall does not mean their mother forgot how to play. A paid rehearsal is still work, even when the audience never arrives.

say: I would keep **live rehearsals** and ask which dates actually pay.
I would request a **written cancellation term** before the next contract.
think: Our **nine-month reserve** makes one cancelled concert manageable.
The **mortgage** still makes unpaid childcare after a cancellation irritating.
do: Keep **chamber calls**, part preparation and Wednesday lessons this season.
Request the **rehearsal cancellation fee** in writing before the next contract.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about existing concert cancellations.
S0.quote: A paid rehearsal is still work, even when the audience never arrives.
fieldNote: Her **nine-month cushion** absorbs a cancelled concert without removing the cost of disrupted childcare.
Her **occasional AI draft** receives manual name and date checks; it is existing use.

steps.text: Keep chamber calls, part preparation and Wednesday lessons this season
Request written rehearsal cancellation fee before the next contract

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the ensemble managers that software may prepare clean parts and publicity faster. We should agree on paid preparation hours before I edit a page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Part preparation brings about a fifth of my income, and a cheaper system could remove most of it. I can still play and teach, but replacing those hours would take work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would ask the manager to put preparation hours and fees into the season contract. In the first year I would attend her paid demonstration of the new score checker, then test it on my own unlabelled part only if the library approves local storage; I would play each change against the original and stop if a note is wrong or the file leaves the library.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel anxious about losing paid preparation hours. Nine months saved buys time, not replacement income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you put a pupil’s part in the checker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A pupil’s name and part stay in the school folder; a test can use my own part without a name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you seek another ensemble now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if our preparation hours actually fall. I would apply for a posted paid clarinet seat, check its written net fee after travel and make sure the call time fits pickup before accepting.

I would ask for a **paid checker demonstration** before testing the tool.
think: Cheaper **part preparation** could remove about a fifth of my income.
Our **nine-month reserve** gives time to seek other paid work.
do: Request **written preparation fees** from the ensemble manager next month.
Test the **score checker** after paid training and library approval, using my nameless part and manual playing; stop on errors or leakage.
Apply for a **posted clarinet seat** if preparation hours fall, only with suitable written net pay and pickup.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a realistic loss of paid preparation work.
S1.quote: Nine months saved buys time, not replacement income.
fieldNote: Her **new checker test** needs paid instruction, approved local storage, a nameless owned part and playing every change.
A second **clarinet seat** needs actual lost hours, a paid posting, net fee after travel and workable pickup.

steps.text: Test approved checker after paid training on nameless part; play changes, stop on errors or leakage
Apply for posted clarinet seat if preparation hours fall, written net pay and pickup fit
Keep chamber playing and Wednesday lessons while preparation work remains paid

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the ensemble that AGI by 2028 may print usable parts in minutes. I want the paid rehearsal schedule signed before we arrange pickups around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the preparation fees to end in 2028, and some commissioned concert notes may go too. Robots able to play clarinet come about three years later, around 2031, but a human chair is no promise of a full season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would total my preparation invoices and request signed rehearsal dates. In the first year after 2028, if paid playing calls also fall, I would apply for a posted music-school clarinet post only if my degree qualifies, its written net pay after travel covers the lost calls and pickup works; I would keep current pupils and playing until a written offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about losing a fifth of my income and perhaps more calls. The reserve gives me a search window, but I would not gamble the mortgage on a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a costly new certificate first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the school requires it and offers a funded place or paid study time. I would not pay tuition from the six months I want to keep untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the school opening is mentioned but not posted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep teaching and playing. An informal mention cannot tell me hours or take-home pay.

I would seek a **posted school opening** if paid playing calls fall.

Apply for a **posted school post** after 2028 playing cuts only if qualified, written net pay covers losses and pickup fits.
Keep **current pupils and playing** until a suitable written offer is signed.
feel: I feel **anxious** about lost preparation fees and possible playing cuts.
S2.quote: An informal mention cannot tell me hours or take-home pay.
fieldNote: Her **preparation income** is threatened in 2028, ahead of 2031 playing robots.
The **school move** needs actual playing cuts, a posted vacancy, degree eligibility, written net pay, pickup and signed offer.

steps.text: Apply after 2028 playing cuts for posted qualifying school role with replacement written net-after-travel and pickup
Keep pupils/playing until written school offer; protect six months of expenses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the arts centre that five years before AGI by 2031 is time to offer something families will pay for. I would propose a small paid clarinet ensemble, not another free concert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Preparation fees could disappear by 2031, but eight families paying for a group might replace part of that work. Robots able to play follow around 2034; I cannot base a class on promises about the orchestra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This spring I would price a six-week beginner ensemble only if the centre offers a room after school pickup and eight families prepay enough for the room, checked loan instruments and my teaching fee. In the first year after 2031 I would repeat it only with eight prepaid places, the room, safe instruments and pickup still available; otherwise I would keep my Wednesday pupils.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel anxious about preparation fees shrinking while I test the first group. Nine months saved lets me try a paid class without depending on an immediate success.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who checks the loan clarinets?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The centre technician would clean and inspect each loan instrument before a child uses it. If that cannot happen, families must bring a sound instrument or I cancel their place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if only five families pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five clarinet-class fees would not cover the room and my teaching time. I would refund them and continue the Wednesday lessons instead of quietly working for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children that ten years before AGI by 2036 is enough to make measured changes. A booked recital with a fee is worth more to us than applause for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Preparation and concert-note fees may end by 2036, while playing robots may threaten seats around 2039. I can build more teaching without treating an empty future calendar as certain today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this year I would move ten percent of each paid preparation invoice into savings after the mortgage, food and instrument repairs, aiming for twelve months while keeping six untouched. In the first year after 2036 I would keep teaching and paid playing, and apply for a posted senior school clarinet opening only if my degree qualifies, written net pay after travel covers lost fees and pickup fits; I would stay in current work until an offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel uneasy about the long horizon, because I have paid work and time to save. If the orchestra cuts chairs, that unease will become anxiety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If preparation invoices stop early, what funds the savings goal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would save only spare paid lesson fees after the household bills. I would leave six months of expenses alone rather than pay for speculative auditions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a grander title for less money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A senior title without written hours and net pay does not meet our mortgage payment.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because preparation fees could disappear before I replace them. Signed rehearsal dates, a posted school opening with real pay and child pickup that works would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who cleans the loan clarinets. A child deserves an instrument that plays, and I will not put my name on an unsafe class.

headlineQuote: A child deserves an instrument that plays, and I will not put my name on an unsafe class.
portrait: At **43**, Dana is an experienced clarinetist with a music degree, two children, a mortgage and nine months saved.
Her higher **musician pay** comes from chamber playing, part preparation and Wednesday lessons.
She tests a **new score checker** only after paid training, library approval, nameless files and playing every change.
A **paid beginner ensemble** needs eight prepayments, a room after pickup, checked instruments and her teaching fee.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase paid preparation work before she replaces the fees.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed rehearsal dates**, a real school vacancy with written pay and workable pickup would give Dana options.
